landing_meta_title: Breathing Comets — The sky is breathing
landing_meta_description: SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 colors of infrared light, every six months. Breathing Comets turns it into a time machine anyone can use, with real mission plates, Gaia astrometry and checked measurements.
landing_hero_lede: SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 colors of infrared light, every six months. We made it a time machine anyone can use — and measured what comets exhale.

landing_s1_title: Pluto was found by blinking two plates.
landing_s1_p1: In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh flipped between two photographic plates of the same patch of sky, taken days apart. Everything that stayed put was a star; the dot that jumped was Pluto.
landing_s1_p2: SPHEREx returns to every part of the sky every six months, so the same trick works across the whole infrared sky.
landing_s1_p3: Barnard's Star moves faster across our sky than any other star. Blink the first and last visits: the crosses are where Gaia predicts it on each date.

landing_s1_alt_b: Crop of the SPHEREx plate around Barnard's Star on {date}, with Gaia-predicted positions marked

landing_s2_p1: SPHEREx has no filter wheel. A linear variable filter sits on each detector, so every row of pixels sees a slightly different wavelength. A star is measured in many colors as the telescope sweeps past it.
landing_s2_p2: The catch: on two visits the same star lands on different rows, so it is seen in a different color ({a} µm versus {b} µm here). Subtract the two frames and almost every star leaves a residue.
landing_s2_p3: Diff λ compares each frame with the static sky at the same wavelength, built from other visits. What survives is what really changed — here, the star that moved.
landing_s2_note: Diff λ reference: static sky at the frame's wavelength from {n} other frames · both panels share one ±5σ color scale
landing_s2_alt_raw: Raw subtraction of two SPHEREx frames at different wavelengths: residues at almost every star
landing_s2_alt_diff: Diff λ of the same frame: only the moving Barnard's Star leaves a positive–negative pair
landing_s2_slider: Drag to compare raw subtraction (left) with Diff λ (right)
landing_s3_title: What the sky is made of.
landing_s3_p1: Each SPHEREx color is a slice of a spectrum. Molecules absorb or glow at their own wavelengths: water, methane, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide all leave fingerprints between 1 and 5 µm, and hydrogen marks itself in sharp lines.
landing_s3_p2: This is a real SPHEREx spectrum of a pair of brown dwarfs, separated from their neighbors with Gaia. Pick a band to see where it shows up.
landing_s3_note: Band definitions: §12.3 of the build guide · shaded widths are the regions annotated, not fits
landing_s3_alt: SPHEREx spectrum of Epsilon Indi B from 0.7 to 5 micrometers, with molecular bands shaded
landing_s3_caption: {name} · deblended SPHEREx reference spectrum · {n} points · flux density in mJy, ±1σ bars
landing_s3_error: The reference spectrum could not be loaded. Nothing is drawn in its place.
landing_s3_pick: Select a band to learn which object in this set shows it.
landing_s3_band_h: Hydrogen recombination lines. None of the five starting targets is used here to demonstrate them; they are marked so you can look for them in the Explorer.
landing_s3_band_h2o: Water absorbs here and again at 1.35 µm, between the brown dwarf’s near-infrared peaks.
landing_s3_band_ch4: Methane absorption: the hallmark of cool T-type brown dwarfs like Epsilon Indi B.
landing_s3_band_co2: Carbon dioxide: the gas comets exhale. The comet measurements live in §4.
landing_s3_band_co: Carbon monoxide, together with methane, shapes the brown dwarf spectrum beyond 4.5 µm; in comets it is a second exhaled gas.
landing_s3_open_target: Open Epsilon Indi B in the Explorer
landing_s4_p1: Near the Sun, a comet's ices turn to gas. In SPHEREx frames the dust glows as a smooth continuum; subtract it and the gas remains, brightest at the carbon dioxide band.
landing_s4_p2: From that glow we estimate how many molecules leave the nucleus each second, always with an uncertainty range and a stated caveat.
landing_s4_note: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is our validation case: its numbers are compared with published measurements in §5.
landing_s4_pending: The 3I/ATLAS plates and gas measurements are not published on this site yet. Until they are, no comet image, gas map or production rate is shown here.
landing_s5_p1: A number is only useful if you know how far to trust it. Every SPHEREx measurement here is compared with an independent reference before it is shown.
landing_s5_comets_pending: Comet comparisons appear here when the 3I/ATLAS package is published.
